newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian PM to try to resolve textile strike.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian PM to try to resolve textile strike.

text.p: Cambodian co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh has agreed to try to resolve a labour dispute between textile workers and a Hong Kong-owned garment factory, lawmakers said on Monday.

Members of Parliament Kem Sokha and Kann Man conveyed the news to scores of striking workers. They had gathered outside the National Assembly on Monday to protest against Tack Fat Garment Ltd's decision to postpone talks with a parliamentary commission on their demands.

Ranariddh has invited the ministers of industry and social affairs and the owners of the garment company to his residence on Tuesday afternoon to discuss the industrial dispute and seek a solution, they said.
Five workers' representatives would be asked to meet members of parliament earlier on Tuesday to prepare a report for the prince on their grievances and demands.
The estimated 150-200 workers dispersed peacefully after hearing from the two members of parliament.
The mostly female work force at Tack Fat's Phnom Penh factory has been on strike since January 3 seeking higher pay, fewer hours and better working conditions.
They have taken part in a series of protests led by opposition leader Sam Rainsy's Khmer Nation Party, including some marred by clashes with police.

A delegation of lawmakers, led by house social welfare and women's affairs committee chairman Kann Man, had been scheduled to meet Tack Fat executives on Monday afternoon to try to resolve differences between the factory workers and owners.

But Kann Man told workers and reporters outside the factory that he had received a letter dated Saturday from Tack Fat saying they wanted to delay the talks indefinitely until they had resolved unspecified internal problems.
Cambodia's parliament last week passed a labour law aimed at protecting the rights of workers and laying down guidelines on the responsibilities of workers and employers.
Government officials said they hoped the measure, when signed into law by King Norodom Sihanouk, would help avoid disputes that they say could damage the country's image and scare off investors.
